title: Stacks and bracket matching
lead: An Essential section on the stack, the last-in, first-out collection, and on using one to check that a string’s brackets balance. Indexing is 0-based: the array stack’s top counts the items on it and names the next free cell. The array-backed stack is the ArrayStack of Section 2.2 in another notation; the linked-list stack pushes and pops at the head of the singly linked list of Section 2.5.
notes: The stack article’s history, hardware stacks, applications and security, its photograph of plates and its UML diagram are left out, as are the bracket article’s counting and enumeration problems.
exercise_notes: Exercism’s matching-brackets and simple-linked-list keep their canonical cases (simple-linked-list as the Python track runs them, last in first out); Donne Martin’s stack challenge keeps his tests; their JavaScript references, and the Kattis tests beyond the five samples and both Kattis references, are the AI’s. OpenDSA’s stack questions wait for the converter of OpenDSA’s exercises, and its push and pop proficiency exercises and the seven Wikibooks stack traces for an answer type that takes a sequence. ODS Exercises 1.2 and 1.3 have no key. Kattis brackets, bracketmatching and GCPC 2023’s loopinvariant were not judged a good fit, and Kattis backspace and throwns are over the cap of two code exercises for the stack. TheAlgorithms’ stack and balanced-parentheses doctests are tests without a printed statement, and trekhleb’s valid-parentheses tests read an empty string as unbalanced and a space as a wrong closing bracket, against Exercism’s statement, so they are not used. pythonds’ end-of-chapter exercises 19 and 30 have no key.

exercises.changes: The tests call run(initial_values, operations), given in the starter, on your LinkedList: push, pop, len for the count, head().value() for a peek, iteration for the list (the last value pushed first) and reversed(). pop and head on an empty list raise EmptyListException("The list is empty.").
exercises.prompt: Write a prototype of the music player application. For the prototype, each song will simply be represented by a number. Given a range of numbers (the song IDs), create a singly linked list. Given a singly linked list, you should be able to reverse the list to play the songs in the opposite order. The linked list is a fundamental data structure in computer science, often used in the implementation of other data structures. The simplest kind of linked list is a singly linked list. That means that each element (or "node") contains data, along with something that points to the next node in the list. If you want to dig deeper into linked lists, check out this article that explains it using nice drawings.

exercises.changes: The tests are the source’s end-to-end test in its three parts, each a list of operations that a given run(ops) plays on your Stack; Stack(Node(5)) starts a stack whose top is 5.
exercises.prompt:
Implement a stack with push, pop, peek, and is_empty methods using a linked list.

If we pop on an empty stack, do we return None? Yes.

Can we assume this fits memory? Yes.

exercises.changes: A solution must run in time linear in the length of the string; the source asks for no bound.
exercises.prompt: Given a string containing brackets [], braces {}, parentheses (), or any combination thereof, verify that any and all pairs are matched and nested correctly. Any other characters should be ignored. For example, "{what is (42)}?" is balanced and "[text}" is not.

answer.grow: (n, rand) => { const o = Array.from({ length: Math.floor(n / 2) }, () => '([{'[rand.int(0, 2)]); const c = { '(': ')', '[': ']', '{': '}' }; return [o.join('') + o.slice().reverse().map((x) => c[x]).join('')]; }

exercises.prompt:
Whenever a programmer starts to learn a Lisp, they think that there are too many parentheses in it. Sophia thinks there are too few, so she is making a programming language with only parentheses. To spice it up a bit, she is also adding square brackets (‘[]’) and curly braces (‘{}’) to the language. Right now, she is struggling to make people use it for production code. Obviously, it has to be because of the bad error messages you get when you mess up the delimiters! Right now, you only get the error message ‘syntax error’ when you mess them up. Any opening delimiter must be closed by the same type of delimiter: ‘(’ is closed with ‘)’, ‘[’ is closed by ‘]’, etc. Sophia wants to improve the error message so that you at least get some help finding out where it all went wrong. Input The input consists of two lines. The first line contains an integer $|L|$, the length of the next line. The next line contains $L$, the program you want to validate. Output Output the character and the $0$-indexed location of the first closing delimiter that does not match with the opening delimiter. If there are no errors, or there are more opening delimiters than closing delimiters, print ‘ok so far’ instead. Limits
  • $1 \leq |L| \leq 200$
  • $L$ contains only the characters ‘()[]{}’ and spaces
  • $L$ does not start with a space character

referents.label: top, the number of items on the array stack and its next free cell
head, the frame on top of the linked stack

top counts the items on the stack now, not every item pushed so far: each pop takes 1 from it. So it is the number pushed less the number popped, and that is also the cell the next push writes to.
